en: The Jātaka,
Great Section (Mahānipāta), Chapter on the Mūgapakkha (The Dumb and Paralysed)
3. The Suvaṇṇasāmaja Jātaka:
“Who has pierced me with an arrow, while I was heedless as a water-carrier?”
"Are you a khattiya, a brahmin, or a vessa?
Who are you that hides and pierces me?
My flesh is not fit to be eaten."
No purpose for eating exists;
by what quality then did you think me one who should be pierced?
Who are you, or whose son are you?
How may we know you?
Answer me properly when asked.
"Why do you hide after piercing me?
"I am the king of the Kāsīs;
I am known as Pīḷiyakkha."
Having abandoned the kingdom out of greed,
I wander about seeking deer;
I am skilled in the art of archery.
Renowned as one of steadfast virtue,
even a nāga would not escape from me when I have come to the field of arrows.
Who are you, or whose son are you?
How may we know you?
And who is your father?
“Proclaim your name and clan.
“I am the son of Nesāda, O venerable sir;
my kinsmen know me as Sāma.”
They addressed him while he was still alive:
"I have gone to sleep as if embraced by my own kin;
I am pierced by a broad-headed arrow."
Like a deer struck by a poisoned arrow,
O King, behold me drenched in my own blood.
The arrow has gone sideways;
see, I am spilling blood.
I, being afflicted, question you.
"Why do you hide after piercing me?
A leopard is killed for its skin;
an elephant is killed for its tusks."
“Now, for what reason did you think of me as one to be pierced?
“A deer was standing nearby.”
He came to the place where the arrow fell;
seeing him, the prince was terrified,
and because of that, anger took possession of me.
“Since I can remember myself,
since I have reached the age of discretion,
the deer do not fear me.”
Even in the forest there are dangers.
Since I have guarded my treasure,
and since I have reached youth;
The deer do not fear me in the forest, even when there are predators;
nor do the timid kimpurisas, O King.
On Mount Gandhamādana,
we go along in mutual delight,
through the mountains and the forests.
The deer do not fear me,
even when there are traps in the forest;
but by what reason indeed—
“The deer are terrified of me.
“O Sāma, that deer is not afraid of you;
why would I speak a falsehood?”
Overcome by lust and greed,
I discharged that arrow at you.
From where indeed have you come, Sāma?
"By whom were you sent?
Go as a messenger to the river;
you have come to Migasammata."
“My parents are blind;
I support them in the great forest.
I provide them with water as their food.”
He has come to Migasammata.
They have a measure of strength;
thus there is life for him.
"Because of the lack of water,
they will surely die blind;
this suffering of mine is not so great."
For this may indeed be obtained by a man;
but that I do not see my mother—
that is more painful to me than this.
This suffering of mine is not so great,
for this could indeed be obtained by a man;
yet that I do not see my father— this is what truly grieves me.
That is more painful to me than this.
Surely that poor mother of mine must be grieving for a long time now.
Whether at midnight or at night,
he flows away like a river;
surely that father of mine is wretched.
For a long time it flows sluggishly;
at midnight or at night,
it flows swiftly like a river.
Through the practice of rising and walking, and by massaging the feet;
we ourselves, dear father, lamenting—
They will wander in the Great Forest.
This too is the second arrow,
which shakes my heart.
"And since I do not see [him] in the darkness,
I think I shall lose my life.
"Do not lament so bitterly;
Sāma has a beautiful appearance;
having become your laborer,
I will support you in the great forest.
I am skilled in archery,
renowned as one of steadfast skill;
having become a laborer, I—
I shall provide for you in the great forest,
seeking the remains of prey from the deer and gathering roots and fruits from the woods.
"Having become a laborer,
I shall support you in the great forest.
Which forest is that, Sāma?"
Wherever your mother and father may be,
I shall support you in such a way that you, in turn, supported them.
“This is my one-footed path, O King,
which lies at the head of my bed;
having gone from here for half a league, [you will find it].”
There is their little home; go from here and support my mother and father.
Homage to you, O King of Kāsi;
homage to you, O Increaser of Kāsi;
my mother and father are blind.
May you support them in the great forest.
I raise my hands in reverent salutation to you;
O King of Kāsi, may it be well with you!
"Tell my mother and father that I have offered my salutation.
Having said this, Sāma—
A youth of beautiful appearance,
he fell into a swoon from the force of the poison and lost consciousness.
That king lamented with much compassion:
“I was one who knew neither aging nor death.”
Today I know this, which I did not know before:
having seen one who has passed away by himself,
there is no non-coming back for one subject to death.
He who challenges me is as if struck by a poisoned arrow;
now that time has come to such a pass, today alone.
He says nothing at all to me.
"Surely I am going to hell;
of this there is no doubt for me."
For then, the evil deed committed becomes a source of misery for a long time;
there will be those who speak of it to him.
A wrongdoer in the village;
in the forest where no humans dwell,
who is there to reproach me?
For actions indeed bring one back;
young men, do not gather in the village,
but [seek] in the forest where there are no people.
"Who indeed will remind me?
That deity vanished on Mount Gandhamādana.
Out of compassion for the king himself,
he spoke these verses:
“It is said, O Great King, that they have come...”
An evil deed was committed;
three innocent father and sons were slain by one and twenty.
Come, I will instruct you so that you may attain a happy rebirth:
support those who are blind in the forest according to the Dhamma.
"I think you have gone to a happy realm.
Having lamented thus, the king uttered much that was full of compassion.
Taking his water-pot,
he set out facing the south.
"Whose sound is this of footsteps?"
It has come from a human being;
this is not the voice of Sāma.
Who are you, O venerable sir?
For the peaceful one indeed walks peacefully, he leads his feet with peace;
this is not the noise of Sāma.
“Who indeed are you, O worthy one?
“I am the king of the Kāsīs,
known by the name Pīḷiyakkha.”
Having abandoned the kingdom out of greed,
I wander about seeking deer;
I am skilled in the art of archery.
Renowned as one of firm virtue,
even a nāga would not escape me when I have reached the place where arrows fall.
“Welcome to you, Great King;
indeed, you have come from afar.
You, a lord, have arrived.”
Proclaim what exists here:
the *tinduka* fruits, the *piyāla* fruits,
the *madhuka*, and the *kāsumārī*.
There are small fruits;
O King, eat the best of them.
This water too is cool.
It has been brought from the heart of the mountain;
drink from it, O Great King,
if you so desire.”
“Blind people in the forest are not able to see;
who indeed has brought fruit for you?
This [fruit] is rightly for one who is not blind.”
“An offering appears to me.
“A youth, young and not yet full-grown,
dark-complexioned and beautiful to behold;”
His long hair was black,
yet its tips were curled and withered;
having brought back fruit, he—
"Taking his water-pot from here,
the water-carrier has gone to the river;
I think he has not yet come far."
“I myself slew that executioner who was your attendant,
whom you spoke of as a prince.”
Smooth and of beautiful appearance;
his long hair is black,
and moreover, it curls at the tips.
"Upon those [skins] smeared with blood lies Sāma, slain by me.
"With whom, Dukūla, do you converse?"
When one says, "Sāma is slain," having heard that "Sāma is slain," my heart trembles.
Like the tender sprout of an assattha tree stirred by the wind,
having heard that Sāma was slain, [he fell].
“My heart trembles.
“Pārikha, this is the King of Kāsi;
he himself has come among those who are regarded as deer.”
"Do not wish for evil upon him who has pierced you with the arrow of anger.
"A beloved son is obtained with difficulty," [said the father].
He who supported his blind parents in the forest—
how could his mind not be provoked to anger when that only son was slain?
“The beloved son, obtained with difficulty,
who supported his blind parents in the forest—
when that only son was slain, [what could be more painful]?”
“The wise have said that there is no anger.
“Do not lament excessively,
saying ‘Sāma is slain!’”
Having become a laborer,
I shall support you in the Great Forest;
and I am skilled in the science of archery.
Known as Daḷhadhamma,
I shall become a laborer and support you in the Great Forest.
While seeking the remains of deer and forest roots and fruits,
I became a laborer.
“I shall carry it to the Brahma Forest.
“This is not the Dhamma, Great King;
this is not appropriate for us.”
“You are our king;
we bow at your feet.
“O hunters, speak the Dhamma!”
"Honour has been rendered by you;
you are our father,
you are our mother, O Pārikā."
"Homage to you, O King of Kāsi!
Homage to you, O Increaser of Kāsi!
We offer our joined palms to you."
Until you have brought him to his senses.
While massaging his feet,
they looked at his face and arms.
“Enduring hardship, we await our time.
This vast forest is infested with predatory beasts.”
He appears as if he were the sky itself;
where Sāma lies slain,
he is like the moon fallen to the earth.
The great forest, strewn with wild beasts,
appears as if it were empty,
where Sāma lies slain.
Like the sun fallen to the earth,
it appears as if it were a vast forest filled with wild beasts, crying out in distress.
Where Sāma lies slain,
covered with dust, amidst the vast wilderness teeming with predatory beasts.
It appears as if it were empty space;
where Sāma lies slain,
right here you shall dwell in the forest.
“Even if there were thousands,
hundreds, and millions there,
no one would cause us any fear.”
"Wild beasts are found in the forest.
Then the King of Kāsi, having taken those blind men to the Great Forest;
Taking him by the hand, he departed for the place where Sāma had been killed;
having seen Sāma fallen there, he...
A little child, covered in dust,
abandoned in the vast forest like the moon fallen to the ground.
Having seen her own little son fallen, covered in dust,
cast away in the vast forest;
Seeing her own son fallen upon the ground like the sun fallen to the earth,
covered in dust and dirt;
Seeing him abandoned in the great forest, fallen by his own hand, they lamented piteously.
Holding her son, who was covered in dust,
she raised her arms and cried out,
"Alas! This is surely unrighteousness!"
"You are indeed deeply negligent,
O Sāma of auspicious appearance, you who,
now that such a time has come, [remain thus]."
"You say nothing at all;
you are indeed burning intensely, O handsome one."
Since time has passed in this way today,
you do not say anything to me;
you are indeed deeply enraged.
Gentleness is beautiful to behold;
that you, having reached such a state today,
do not say anything at all to me.
"You are indeed fast asleep,
O handsome youth, you who remain thus while the day has already passed."
"You do not say anything at all.
You are indeed deeply despondent,
O you of beautiful appearance."
Since time has passed in this way today,
you do not say anything to me.
[Your] matted hair is wrinkled and covered in dust.
Who now will provide guidance?
This Sāma has passed away,
he who was the attendant for the blind.
"Who will take up my broom and sweep this hermitage?
This Sāma has passed away."
He is the attendant for the blind.
Who now will bathe him with cold and warm water?
Sāma has passed away,
he who was the attendant of the blind.
Who now will provide them with food?
And forest roots and fruits;
this Sāma has passed away,
he who was the attendant of the blind.”
Seeing her own son fallen there,
covered in dust and dirt, she was distressed by grief for her child.
The mother spoke the truth: "By that truth,
by which this Sāma was formerly a practitioner of the Dhamma..."
By this utterance of truth,
may the poison of Sāma be destroyed!
By that truth which this Sāma possesses—
I was a celibate student in the past;
by this utterance of truth,
may the poison of Sāma be destroyed.
By that truth by which this Sāma was formerly a speaker of truth— by this utterance of truth, may he be released from the snake's poison.
Let the poison be destroyed by Sāma!
By that truth that this Sāma was a supporter of his mother and father;
By this utterance of truth,
may Sāma’s poison be destroyed!
By that truth wherein this Sāma [lives]...
I am one who honors the elders in my family;
by this utterance of truth,
may Sāma’s poison be destroyed!
By this truth that Sāma is dearer to me than life itself— by this utterance of truth, may my arm be restored!
Let the poison be destroyed by his own tranquility!
Whatever merit has been performed,
both by me and by my father, may it be for you.
"By all that wholesome merit,
may the poison kill Sāma.
Having seen Sāma fallen, [he said:]
Seeing his little son covered in dust, the father,
distressed by grief for his son,
spoke these words of truth.
“By the truth that this Sāma was formerly a practitioner of the Dhamma,
by this utterance of truth— ”
Let the poison be destroyed by Sāma!
By that truth that this Sāma was formerly a practitioner of the holy life (brahmacārī), [let the poison be destroyed].
By this utterance of truth,
may Sāma’s poison be destroyed!
By that truth which this Sāma possesses—
In former times he was a speaker of truth;
by this utterance of truth,
may the poison of Sāma be destroyed.
By that truth by which this Sāma was one who supported his mother and father— by this utterance of truth, [may my arm be restored].
Let the poison destroy Sāma!
By that truth that this Sāma honors his elders in the family, [let it destroy the poison].
By this utterance of truth,
may the poison of Sāma be destroyed.
By that truth which this Sāma possesses, [may he be freed].
Life is dearer to me than anything else;
by this utterance of truth,
may the poison be destroyed for Sāma.
Whatever merit has been performed,
both by me and by your mother—
by all that wholesome deed, [may there be success].
"Let the poison be destroyed by calmness.
That deity vanished on Mount Gandhamādana.
Out of compassion for Sāma,
you spoke this truth:
"I [lived] on Mount Gandhamādana..."
She has dwelt with me for a long time;
there is no one else more dear to me than she, even among my own sons.
By this utterance of truth,
may Sāma’s poison be destroyed.
May all forests be filled with fragrance.
On Mount Gandhamādana;
by this utterance of truth,
may Sāma’s poison be destroyed!
While they were lamenting with much piteous cries,
Sāma quickly rose up.
“Young and of auspicious appearance.
“I am well, sir; may it be well with you.
I have emerged safely.”
"Do not lament excessively;
address me with gentle words.
"Welcome to you, Great King!"
Moreover, you are welcome;
you have arrived as a lord—
proclaim whatever is here.
Tinduka fruits, piyāla fruits,
madhuka, and kāsumārī;
small-sized fruits—
"O King, enjoy this excellent,
choice food. I have cool water brought from the heart of the mountain."
"Therefore drink from it as well, O Great King, if you so desire.
"I am bewildered; I am utterly confused."
All directions have become bewildered to me;
I have seen you as a dead corpse, Sāma—
what indeed are you, Sāma, that you live?
“Even while living, O Great King,
a man who is in intense pain,
whose mind and intentions are directed elsewhere— ”
One perceives the dead as living.
Even while living, O Great King,
a person may experience intense agony.
When it has reached cessation and is stilled,
one imagines that which is living to be dead;
he who [neglects] his mother or father...
A mortal nourishes [the world] through Dhamma;
even the gods seek to heal that man who supports his mother and father.
The mortal who supports his mother or father in accordance with the Dhamma is praised right here in this world.
"And having passed away, he rejoices in heaven.
"At this, I become even more bewildered;
all directions are clouded for me."
“I go to you for refuge, O Sāma;
may you also be my refuge.
“Practice the Dhamma, O Great King.”
O Kshatriya, toward your mother and father;
having practiced the Dhamma here,
O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King,
toward your sons and wives, O Kshatriya;
having practiced the Dhamma here in this world, [you will attain happiness after death].
O King, you shall go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King,
toward your friends and companions, O Kshatriya.
Having practiced the Dhamma here,
O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, Great King.
Regarding vehicles and forces:
having practiced the Dhamma here,
O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King,
in villages and in towns;
having practiced the Dhamma here in this world, [you will attain happiness after death].
O King, you shall go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King,
throughout the kingdoms and the provinces.
Having practiced the Dhamma here,
O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, Great King.
And among recluses and brahmins;
having practiced the Dhamma here,
O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King,
toward the beasts and birds, O Kshatriya;
having practiced the Dhamma here in this world, [you will attain happiness after death].
O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King;
the Dhamma, when practiced, brings happiness.
Having practiced the Dhamma here,
O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, Great King.
“O King, together with Indra and Brahmā,
the gods have attained heaven through their well-performed deeds;
do not be negligent regarding the Dhamma.”
The Third Jātaka: The Golden Sāma.
